texts.text: BACKGROUND: Whether it is effective and safe to extend the time window of intravenous thrombolysis up to 24 hours after the last known well is unknown. We aimed to determine the efficacy and safety of tenecteplase in Chinese patients with acute ischemic stroke due to large/medium vessel occlusion within an extended time window.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: METHODS: Patients with ischemic stroke presenting 4.5 to 24 hours from the last known well, with a favorable penumbral profile and an associated large/medium vessel occlusion, were randomized 1:1 to either 0.25 mg/kg tenecteplase or the best medical treatment. A favorable penumbral profile was defined as a hypoperfusion lesion volume to infarct core volume ratio >1.2, with an absolute volume difference >10 mL, and an ischemic core volume <70 mL. The primary outcome was the achievement of major reperfusion without symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage within 24 to 48 hours post-randomization. Major  reperfusion  was  defined  as  the  restoration  of  blood  flow  of  >50%  of  the  involved  ischemic  territory.  Secondary outcomes included recanalization,  infarct  growth,  major  neurological  improvements,  change  in  the  National  Institutes  of Health Stroke Scale score, hemorrhagic transformation within 24 to 48 hours, systemic bleeding at discharge, and modified Rankin Scale (score 0-1, score 0-2, score 5-6, and modified Rankin Scale distribution) at 90 days. The comparison of the primary outcome between groups was conducted using modified Poisson regression with a log-link function and robust error variance, adjusted for time from the last known well to randomization, the site of vessel occlusion, and planned endovascular treatment.

texts.orig: RESULTS: Among 224 enrolled patients, 111 were assigned to receive tenecteplase and 113 to receive the best medical treatment (including 23% [n=26] of participants who received intravenous tissue-type plasminogen activator). The mean (SD) age of the tenecteplase group and the best medical treatment group was 64.2 (10.4) and 63.6 (11.0) years old, with 72.1% (n=80) and 70.8% (n=80) male enrolled, respectively. A proportion of 54.9% (n=123) of patients were transferred to  the  catheter  room  for  preplanned  endovascular  treatment.  The  primary  outcome  occurred  in  33.3%  (n=37)  of  the tenecteplase group versus 10.8% (n=12) in the best medical treatment group (adjusted relative risk, 3.0 [95% CI, 1.6-5.7]; P =0.001). Tenecteplase significantly increased the recanalization rate compared with the best medical treatment (35.8% [n=39] versus 14.3% [n=16], adjusted relative risk, 2.5 [95% CI, 1.4-4.4]; P =0.002). There were no significant differences in clinical efficacy outcomes or rates of hemorrhagic transformation between the groups.

texts.orig: R eperfusion therapy, including intravenous thrombolysis  and  endovascular treatment (EVT), is the most effective treatment for patients with acute ischemic stroke (AIS). Extending the time window for reperfusion therapy and thus making more patients with AIS eligible for reperfusion therapy has been one of the research priorities in stroke for decades. Through advanced imaging selection, the time window for EVT has been extended to 24 hours after the last known well. 1-4  However, compared with EVT trials using advanced imaging in the early window, outcomes in the late window for patients with AIS seem less favorable. This discrepancy could be due to the lower percentage (<10%) of late-window patients with  AIS  receiving  alteplase  treatment  compared  with nearly 100% in the early window. 3-5 This disparity underscores  the  potential  for  intravenous  thrombolysis  to improve outcomes for late-window patients.

texts.orig: Eligible patients ranged from 18 to 80, with a premorbid modified Rankin Scale (mRS) of 0 to 2. They presented with AIS within  4.5  to  24  hours  after  last  known  well  and  showed  a clinically significant acute neurological deficit, as judged by the investigators and quantified by a National Institutes of Health Stroke  Scale  (NIHSS)  score.  Eligibility  was  also  required  to meet the dual-target criteria on baseline multimodal imaging. The dual-target criteria were defined as large or medium vessel occlusion in the anterior circulation on baseline computed tomography  angiography  (CTA),  and  a  favorable  penumbral mismatch profile on baseline computed tomography perfusion (CTP). Large or medium vessel occlusion encompassed occlusions in the extracranial or intracranial segments of the internal carotid artery, the first or second segments of the middle cerebral artery, and the first or second segments of the anterior cerebral artery on CTA. In cases of tandem occlusions, the distal occlusion site was considered the culprit for assessing the efficacy of tenecteplase. A favorable penumbral mismatch profile on CTP was determined by a hypoperfusion lesion volume (delay time [DT]  >3 seconds) to infarct core volume (relative cerebral blood flow <30%) 15,16 ratio >1.2, with an absolute volume difference >10 mL, and an ischemic core volume under 70 mL, which was generated by an automated real-time perfusion volumetric software, AutoMIStar (Apollo Medical Imaging Technology, Melbourne, Victoria, Australia).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The primary outcome combined efficacy and safety, defined as major reperfusion at initial catheter angiography or on a 4- to 6-hour repeat CTP, without sICH occurred 24 to 48 hours after randomization. Major reperfusion was defined as the restoration of blood flow of >50% of the involved ischemic territory. For patients without preplanned emergent EVT, major reperfusion was defined as the hypoperfusion lesion volume (DT >3 seconds) of the 4- to 6-hour repeat CTP decreased to <50% of  the  hypoperfusion  lesion  volume  of  the  baseline  CTP.  For patients with preplanned emergent EVT, major reperfusion was assessed as a modified Treatment In Cerebral Ischemia score 2b to 3 at the initial catheter angiography. 18  sICH was defined as any intracranial hemorrhage causing a ≥ 4-point increase in the NIHSS score from baseline.

texts.orig: Sample size calculation was primarily based on the   EXTEND-IA TNK trial  (T enecteplase  Versus  Alteplase  Before  Endovascular Therapy  for  Ischemic  Stroke) results, 19 where  22%  of  patients receiving  intravenous  tenecteplase  and  10%  of  those  treated with intravenous alteplase reached major reperfusion. In addition, in  both  groups,  1%  of  patients  developed  sICH.  Therefore,  we hypothesized that 21% of patients in the tenecteplase group and 7% in the best medical treatment group would attain the primary outcome of major reperfusion without sICH. This trial design aimed for  an  85% power to detect between-group differences with a 2-sided type I error of 0.05, accounting for a 5% dropout rate, resulting in a total of 224 patients (112 patients in each group).

texts.orig: CHABLIS-T II has the following limitations. First, the sample size was limited, so a composite safety and efficacy  primary  end  point  was  set  instead  of  long-term functional outcomes (mRS at 90 days). In addition, we expected the effect on the functional outcome of EVT to obscure any potential difference between tenecteplase and  the  best  medical  treatment  including  alteplase, which was shown in TIMELESS. 12  Second, the patients enrolled were highly selected, only accounting for 3.6% of the candidates screened. Third, the criteria of hypoperfusion lesion in CHABLIS-T II was defined using DT >3 seconds rather than the widely applied time to maximum >6 seconds. Though previous studies have proven that  the  threshold  of  DT  >3  seconds  is  as  accurate as  time  to  maximum  >6  seconds  when  defining  acute hypoperfused lesion, 15,16  a post hoc analysis using time to maximum >6 seconds may be helpful to the generalizability of this study. Furthermore, this trial adopted a mismatch volume threshold of 10 mL and a ratio of 1.2, which allowed for the inclusion of a larger patient population  compared  with  the  more  stringent  criteria  (mismatch volume of 15 mL and ratio of 1.8). As a result, the findings of the trial were more broadly generalizable. Fourth, reperfusion status was assessed through 2 imaging modalities, CTP or digital subtracted angiography, for patients with or without preplanned EVT. However, our previous study has proven that both imaging modalities could reliably assess the reperfusion status of patients with  large  vessel  occlusion(s). 30 Fifth,  only  54.9%  of patients  underwent  preplanned  EVT  treatment.  Major reasons  for  this  low  EVT  rate  included  the  inability  to obtain informed consent and bleeding concerns from the neurointerventionalists. Sixth, contradiction remained to be explained concerning the analysis of outcomes, especially  for  the  result  that  no  difference  in  infarct  growth was demonstrated between treatment groups, although tenecteplase induced a higher possibility of reperfusion. Seventh, time delay existed from thrombolysis administration to EVT, which might significantly impact the functional outcome of patients. Therefore, an improvement in the treatment workflow is needed.

texts.orig: In conclusion, administered at a dose of 0.25 mg/kg intravenously,  tenecteplase  increased  reperfusion  without  sICH  in  patients  with  ischemic  stroke  selected  by imaging in late-time window treatment but did not change clinical outcomes at 90 days. To translate sufficient and safe reperfusion into an improvement in functional outcome, other medical scenarios may be considered, such as using tenecteplase for thrombolysis at primary stroke centers followed by transporting patients to comprehensive stroke centers for EVT. Together with TRACE-III, 11 TIMELESS, 12   and  the  ETERNAL-LVO  trial  (Extending the Time Window for Tenecteplase by Effective Reperfusion in Patients With Large Vessel Occlusion;  https:// www.clinicaltrials.gov; Unique identifier: NCT04454788), CHABLIS-T  II  provides  new  evidence  of  intravenous tenecteplase treatment in patients with acute stroke in an extended time window.
